Contribution We study the Gumbel watermarking procedure ( Algorithm 1 ), but replace the detection test proposed by Aaronson (2022) with a new test that is theoretically more statistically efficient. We prove nearly matching problem-dependent upper and lower bounds on the number of tokens needed to detect watermarked text. Our bounds are in terms of an entropy-like quantity of the distribution of next-token distributions. The lower bound applies to all watermarking schemes in the same framework (to be explained) and hence the Gumbel scheme combined with the new detector is (in a certain sense) nearly optimal. Related work There are now a huge variety of schemes for watermarking language models, with a range of desiderata and analysis objectives ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Piet et al., 2025 ) . A relatively recent summary of the current state-of-the-art can be found in the review by Ji et al. (2025) , but the field is growing incredibly rapidly. Some schemes are distortionary in the sense that they change the distribution of the model ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) while others are non-distortionary ( Aaronson, 2022 ; Dathathri et al., 2024 ) . Our work is based on the non-distortionary Gumbel watermarking scheme proposed and analysed by Aaronson (2022) . Aaronson (2022) used a detection mechanism based on a different statistic than the one proposed here and proved that detection occurs with high probability once n = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / δ ) / H ¯ 2 ) n=\Omega(\log(1/\delta)/ ar{H}^{2}) with H ¯  ar{H} the average entropy (see Eq. 1 ). This is the detection time that seems to be obtained most naturally when the concentration analysis used is not variance-aware ( Christ et al., 2024 ) . Huang et al. (2023) theoretically study watermarking procedures that are both distortion free and distortionary. Perhaps the most relevant of their results is a proof that when P t = p P_{t}=p is constant, then detection is possible if n = Ω ⁡ ( log ⁡ ( 1 / H ⁡ ( p ) ) ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / δ ) / H ⁡ ( p ) ) n=\Omega(\log(1/H(p))\log(1/\delta)/H(p)) and that this is optimal. Like us, Li et al. (2025a) also examine the problem of refining the detection of Gumbel watermarking (and the scheme by Kuditipudi et al. (2023) ). They propose a model-agnostic detector that is optimal in an asymptotic minimax framework where P t P_{t} is assumed to satisfy max a ∈ Σ ⁡ P t ​ ( a ) ≤ 1 − Δ \max_{a\in\Sigma}P_{t}(a)\leq 1-\Delta for some user-provided constant Δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \Delta\in(0,1) . On the one hand, they are able to establish a kind of exact optimality. On the other hand, thanks to the minimax nature of their optimality definition, it is unclear if their method achieves the same kind of near-optimal problem-dependent detection efficiency as our proposal. Our statistical test is inspired by the classical literature on goodness-of-fit tests, and particularly the Anderson–Darling test ( Anderson and Darling, 1952 ) . Goodness-of-fit tests have been used for Gumbel watermarking by He et al. (2025) . Li et al. (2025b) also use goodness-of-fit tests for detection. They primarily focus on a more complicated version of the problem where some of the text has been generated by an LLM but other parts are human-generated. Nevertheless, they prove a kind of optimality in certain scenarios. At the same time, their results seem incomparable to ours. 6 Discussion Experiments You surely noticed the absence of experiments. Our brief tests showed the power law detector indeed outperforms the exponential detector in synthetically crafted examples where the theory says it should (e.g., Example 8 ). Unfortunately, however, its performance on language data seems to be slightly worse, presumably due to the additional logarithmic factor and/or constant factors. There may be ways to improve the proposed statistic to get the best of both worlds. Most naively one can combine both detectors with a union bound, but better methods might be possible.
